# Bichromatic Imaging of Single Molecules in an Optical Tweezer Array

Connor M. Holland,1 Yukai Lu,1, 2 and Lawrence W. Cheuk1, ∗

1Department of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544 USA 2Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544 USA (Dated: August 26, 2022)

We report on a novel bichromatic ﬂuorescent imaging scheme for background-free detection of single CaF molecules trapped in an optical tweezer array. By collecting ﬂuorescence on one optical transition while using another for laser-cooling, we achieve an imaging ﬁdelity of 97.7(2)% and a non-destructive detection ﬁdelity of 95.5(6)%. We characterize loss mechanisms of our scheme, many of which are generically relevant to the ﬂuorescent detection of trapped molecules, including two-photon decay and admixtures of higher excited states that are induced by the trapping light.

Single molecules trapped in rearrangeable arrays of optical tweezers have been proposed as a platform for quantum simulation, quantum information processing, and precision measurements [1–4]. Compared to the platform of neutral atoms in optical tweezer arrays [5–9], which has been very successful in a wide variety of quantum applications [10–16], molecules in tweezer arrays offer new capabilities thanks to their rich internal structure and long-range electric dipolar interactions in long-lived states [17, 18]. These features have spurred experimental eﬀorts to create single molecules in tweezer arrays via coherent assembly from constituent atoms [19–23] and through direct laser-cooling [24–26]. The latter approach of directly laser-cooling has the advantage of potentially higher loading rates and higher detection ﬁdelities, because individual molecules can be directly cooled and read out optically through cycling hundreds of photons. Crucially, it appears to be a general technique that could be extended to polyatomic molecules [27–31]. Laser-cooled molecules in optical tweezers may be non-destructively detected through ﬂuorescent imaging. However, because optical tweezers have limited trap depths, cooling is needed to counteract the recoil heating due to photon scattering. To date, Λ-imaging has been the only technique that provides both cooling and the ﬂuorescence needed to detect single molecules [24, 32]. Nevertheless, it comes with a side eﬀect. Stray laser-cooling light can lead to signiﬁcant detection backgrounds that reduce detection ﬁdelities. A strategy to circumvent this problem is to use two optical transitions, one for lasercooling and the other for inducing ﬂuorescence. In such a bichromatic scheme, background-free detection can be achieved by spectrally ﬁltering out stray laser-cooling light. This approach has been successfully used to image single atoms in optical lattices and optical tweezers [7–9, 33–35]. For molecules, bichromatic imaging schemes have also been demonstrated for laser-cooled ensembles [31, 36], but not with single molecule resolution. In this paper, we demonstrate a high-ﬁdelity bichromatic imaging scheme for single CaF molecules trapped in optical tweezers. The molecules are transported to the focus of a high numerical aperture microscope objective (NA=0.65) and then loaded in the presence of Λ-cooling light into a linear array of 20 identical optical tweezer traps [40]. The tweezer traps are created from focused beams of 781 nm light propagating through the objective along −ˆz (Fig. 1(b)). The Λ-cooling light is applied along all three directions (±ˆx, ±ˆy and ±ˆz), while the X −B excitation light avoids the objective axis (ˆz) and only propagates roughly in the ˆx −ˆy plane. The resulting X −B ﬂuorescence is collected through the microscope objective and imaged onto an EMCCD camera with an overall eﬃciency of 0.049(2). Dichroic ﬁlters in the imaging path remove the Λ-cooling light, X −A ﬂuorescence, and stray optical tweezer light. As shown in Fig. 1(c), the average images obtained using bichromatic imaging reveal the presence of molecules in the optical tweezer array. Optimizing for maximal survival at a ﬁxed X −B light intensity of I = 12(1)mW/cm2, we ﬁnd Λ- cooling parameters similar to those previously reported for Λ-imaging [24]. At optimal parameters, we obtain an imaging lifetime of τ = 148(14) ms, and a X −B photon scattering rate of Γsc = 1.95(4) × 104 s−1. To evaluate the imaging performance, we ﬁrst construct histograms of the total camera counts in cropped image regions surrounding each tweezer (Fig. 1(c)). The histograms reveal a bimodal distribution (Fig. 1(d)), with the two peaks corresponding to tweezer instances that are empty and occupied. We classify tweezer instances below (above) a threshold θ as empty (occupied). We describe the classiﬁcation errors by two probabilities, ϵ10 and ϵ01, which correspond to the probabilities of incorrectly classifying an occupied tweezer as empty and vice versa. The total misclassiﬁcation probability is dependent on the average occupation p and is given by ϵ(p) = p ϵ10+(1−p)ϵ01. We deﬁne the imaging ﬁdelity f as probability of correctly classifying a tweezer when the occupation probability is 0.5, i.e. f = 1 −ϵopt(0.5), at the optimal threshold θopt. By applying a rescaling procedure to histograms (details in [40]), we obtain the classiﬁcation errors ϵ10 and ϵ01 for 30 ms-long images, from which we extract an imaging ﬁdelity of f = 0.977(2) (Fig. 2(a)). During the images, ≈35 photons are collected per molecule, which is well above the background of ≈0.3 photons per tweezer. A second metric for single molecule detection is the non-destructive detection ﬁdelity fND, which we deﬁne as the probability that a tweezer initially classiﬁed as occupied remains occupied following imaging. This metric is relevant to rearranging molecules into defect-free arrays, since the success probability of creating an array of size N is limited by (fND)N. Unlike the imaging ﬁdelity f, the non-destructive detection ﬁdelity fND primarily depends on ϵ01, which is approximately equivalent to the false-positive rate. The detection threshold θ can therefore be increased to reduce ϵ01 at the expense of increasing ϵ10, which is the probability of rejecting occupied tweezers. In addition to the classiﬁcation errors ϵ10 and ϵ01, fND is also aﬀected by the survival probability of molecules following detection. Thus, the imaging duration should be chosen to balance between minimizing imaging loss and maximizing molecular ﬂuorescence;

Since fND is the fraction of molecules initially classiﬁed as occupied that survives detection, it can be directly measured with repeated imaging. To determine fND, we image the molecules twice, ﬁrst with a 10 ms-long bichromatic pulse, and then with a 30 ms-long pulse [40]. As expected, fND increases at the expense of rejecting occupied tweezer instances (Fig. 2(b)). At a moderate data rejection rate of fR = 15%, we achieve a non-destructive detection ﬁdelity of fND = 95.5(6)%. Both the imaging ﬁdelity and non-destructive detection ﬁdelity are comparable to or better than previously reported [24, 25], and are suﬃcient for experiments with small-scale rearrangeable optical tweezer arrays. Having characterized bichromatic imaging ﬁdelities, we next compare the bichromatic imaging performance to that of single-color Λ-imaging. We ﬁrst examine the dependence of the bichromatic loss rate γ = 1/τ on the X −B imaging power I and ﬁnd that it increases with I. In particular, the excess loss rate beyond Λ-imaging loss, given by γexcess = γ(I) −γ(0), is observed to increase linearly with I (Fig. 3(a)). To allow further comparison with single-color Λ-imaging, we deﬁne an imaging ﬁgure-of-merit η = Γscτ, where Γsc is the ﬂuorescence rate of imaging photons and τ is the imaging lifetime. We note that η measures how many photons can be collected before a molecule is lost. At high X −B powers, η saturates to ≈3 × 103, roughly 10 times lower than that of Λ-imaging (η ≈40 × 103) (Fig. 3(b)). Each scattered X −B photon during bichromatic imaging gives ≈10 times more loss compared to each X −A photon scattered during Λ-imaging. We next explore possible mechanisms that could explain the excess loss rate γexcess observed during bichromatic imaging. For comparison, X −B light heats the molecules to 310(30) µK in 10 ms in the absence of Λ-cooling. We next investigate loss into undetected rotational states, which can be separated into parity-conserving and parity-changing loss. One mechanism of parityconserving loss arises even under Λ-cooling alone. Molecules oﬀ-resonantly excited to A2Π1/2 (v = 0, J = 3/2, 5/2, +) can decay into X2Σ (v = 0, N = 3) (Fig. 4(b)). We ﬁnd that adding a rotational repumping laser addressing the X2Σ (v = 0, N = 3) →B2Σ (v = 0, N = 2) transition greatly reduces this rotational loss to negligible levels [40]. We verify that removing this rotational repumping laser does not signiﬁcantly increase the excess loss during bichromatic imaging [40]. We note that vibrational-changing loss into X2Σ (v = 1, N = 3) should be negligible because of the highly diagonal Franck- Condon factors of the A2Π1/2 (v = 0) →X2Σ(v = 0) and B2Σ (v = 0) →X2Σ(v = 0) transitions [40]. We next quantify parity-changing rotational loss, which could arise from stray electric ﬁelds mixing in excited states of opposite parity or molecules decaying via the two-photon pathway B →A →X (Fig. 4(d)). The admixture of opposite-parity states due to stray electric ﬁelds is expected to be much higher for the A2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2, +) state compared to that for the B2Σ(v = 0, N = 0) state because of the much smaller A2Π1/2 Λ-doublet splitting compared to the B2Σ rotational splitting separating opposite parity states. In combination with the much higher scattering rate of X −A cooling photons, we conclude that the excess loss during bichromatic imaging cannot be due to stray electric ﬁelds. To measure the loss due to two-photon decay, which results in molecules accumulating in the opposite par-

ity rotational states X2Σ(v = 0, N = 0, 2), we directly track the X2Σ (v = 0, N = 0, F = 1) population during bichromatic imaging using a sequence of resonant blow-out pulses, microwave sweeps and optical pumping pulses [40]. As a function of the imaging duration t, the X2Σ (v = 0, N = 0, F = 1) population initially rises before decaying slowly (Fig. 4(c)). Using a rate-equation model with parameters measured separately [40], we extract a B →A branching ratio of 7.9(16) × 10−5, slightly lower than the theoretically predicted value of 1.3 × 10−4 [41], but much higher than previously measured in free-space in a molecular beam (9(2) × 10−6) [42]. The branching ratio indicates an A −B transition dipole moment of |dAB| = 0.30(3)ea0, which is 0.07 ea0 smaller than theoretically predicted [41]. Lastly, we investigate loss that arises from admixtures of the the higher-lying C states into the excited B states due to the optical tweezer light. Although the trapping light is far oﬀ-resonant from any optical transition involving the ground X2Σ(v = 0) state, it is relatively closed-detuned to the B −C transitions. Suﬃcient coupling between the B and C states can give rise to observable losses through two mechanisms. First, strong anti-trapping of molecules in the B state can lead to heating during bichromatic imaging and subsequent loss of molecules out of the tweezer traps. This anti-trapping occurs since the tweezer light is blue-detuned from the strongest B2Σ(v = 0) −C2Π(v = 0, 1, 2) transitions. We have, however, already ruled out heating from our thermometry measurements. Second, admixture of the C state into the B state can lead to decay into unaddressed rotational and vibrational states during imaging, since the C state can decay via multi-photon pathways and the X −C Franck-Condon factors are non-diagonal (Fig. 4(g)). At ﬁrst glance, the theoretically predicted value of the B −C transition dipole moment |dth BC| = 7.33 ea0 [43] suggests that at our tweezer wavelength, the polarizabilities of the X and B state diﬀer in magnitude by ∼20, and the B state experiences a large and opposite ac Stark shift. Speciﬁcally, at the tweezer depth used for imaging, the predicted peak diﬀerential ac Stark shift is ∆th XB ≈h × 600 MHz. The corresponding imaging loss rate into dark rovibrational states is predicted to be 6 times higher than what we observe. This motivates a careful measurement of |dBC|. We do so by measuring the diﬀerential ac Stark shift between the X and B states ∆XB, which is sensitive to d2 BC. ∆XB is measured via loss spectroscopy by illuminating the molecules with light on the X −B transition. Peak loss is observed when the X −B light is on resonant with the Stark-shifted transitions. Taking into account that the observed diﬀerential ac Stark shift is averaged over the trap, we infer a peak diﬀerential ac Stark shift of ∆XB = h×78(2) MHz at the center of the tweezer traps. This is much smaller than ∆th XB and provides a ﬁrst indication that |dBC| is smaller than predicted. When the tweezer light is adjusted to 782.0 nm, we observe minimal dependence of ∆XB on the tweezer intensity (Fig. 4(e)). We next keep the tweezer intensity ﬁxed at the imaging intensity and vary the wavelength of the tweezer light around 781 nm. As shown in Fig. 4(f), the diﬀerential ac Stark shift ∆XB displays two dispersive features, which originate from the B2Σ(v = 0) −C2Π1/2(v = 3) and B2Σ(v = 0) −C2Π3/2(v = 3) transitions. The amplitudes of the dispersive features directly measure fBC,03d2 BC, where fBC,03 is the Frank-Condon factor between B2Σ(v = 0) and C2Π(v = 3) states. Fitting the dispersive lineshapes and using fBC,03 calculated from spectroscopic data [45, 46], we ﬁnd a B −C transition dipole moment of |dBC| = 2.0(1) ea0, much smaller than the predicted value of |dth BC| = 7.33 ea0 [43]. Assuming that C-state decays always lead to loss, the admixture of the C state into the B state leads to an additional loss rate of β2ΓCPB, where β is the amplitude of the C-state admixture, PB is the fraction of molecules excited to the B state, and ΓC is the decay rate of the C state. β can be determined from the measured ac Stark shifts, and PB = Γsc/ΓB, where Γsc is the measured X −B scattering rate and ΓB is the B-state linewidth. We estimate ΓC by assuming that C2Π molecules decay only via E1 transitions, i.e. ΓC = ΓC,rad [40]. Using the measured value of |dBC|, along with theoretical values of |dXC| and |dAC|, we determine a radiative decay rate ΓC,rad of 2π×5.3(2) MHz. The resulting estimated excess loss rates are much smaller than observed, as shown in Fig. 4(h). Away from the two B2Σ(v = 0) −C2Π(v = 3) resonances, we only account for ∼30% of the observed excess loss rate γexcess. This suggests that either fBC,03 is different than calculated or that additional loss mechanisms exist. The former is unlikely since extensive spectroscopy has been performed on the X −A, X −B and X −C −D systems of CaF [45, 46]. In addition, away from the two dispersive features, the background value of ∆XB is only weakly sensitive to the B −C Franck-Condon factors, and is consistent with our extracted value of dBC. Possible additional loss mechanisms include pre-dissociation of the C states, which would lead to ΓC > ΓC,rad, and photoionization of B-state molecules that could arise for example from absorption of an X −A photon and a tweezer photon [47]. B-state molecules could also be oﬀ- resonantly excited into high-lying Rydberg states that have large decay rates [48], potentially giving rise to appreciable imaging losses. In summary, we have demonstrated a background-free bichromatic imaging scheme for single CaF molecules in

an array of µm-sized optical tweezer traps. We achieve an imaging ﬁdelity and non-destructive detection ﬁdelity suﬃcient for small-scale rearrangeable molecular tweezer array experiments. Our scheme could be extended to other laser-coolable molecules, and could be useful in experiments where stray laser-cooling light is diﬃcult to avoid. To understand the limitations of bichromatic imaging, we have characterized multiple loss mechanisms. We note that the explored mechanisms are not speciﬁc to bichromatic imaging, and are generically relevant to ﬂuorescent detection of trapped molecules. Lastly, our investigations have provided a new measurement of the A −B transition dipole moment and the ﬁrst measurement of the B −C transition dipole moment of CaF. The latter was obtained through a novel method relying on dispersive ac Stark shifts, which allows measurement of transition dipole moments between excited states with arbitrarily small Frank-Condon factors. Extensions of this method could potentially be applied to investigate optical cycling in polyatomic molecules [49, 50].

## I. APPARATUS DESCRIPTION

## A. Overview

The experimental apparatus consists of three vacuum chambers connected in series, which we call the molecular source chamber, the intermediate chamber, and the science chamber (details in [1]). A cryogenic buﬀer gas beam (CBGB) of CaF is ﬁrst generated in the molecular source chamber and passes through the intermediate chamber into the science chamber. The molecular beam is optically slowed and captured into a magnetooptical trap (MOT) at the center of the science chamber. Following magneto-optical trapping, molecules are transferred into a large-volume attractive optical trap, and ultimately into the optical tweezers, all with the aid of Λ-cooling. We describe these steps in detail in the following sections.

## B. Description of Laser Beams Used

To aid the discussion in subsequent sections, we describe the laser beams used for slowing, magneto-optical trapping, sub-Doppler cooling and ﬂuorescent imaging. The slowing beam consists of light addressing the X 2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) →B 2Σ(v = 0, N = 0) transition (λ = 531.0 nm). Sidebands addressing the ground state hyperﬁne manifolds are created via an electrooptical modulator (EOM) driven by a waveform created via computer-generated holography [2]. The slowing beam also contains the v = 1, 2, 3 vibrational repumping light (X 2Σ(v = 1, 2, 3, N = 1) →A 2Π1/2(v = 0, 1, 2, J = 1/2, +)). For the vibrational repumpers, hyperﬁne sidebands are generated using overdriven electrooptical modulators (EOMs). The main cooling light (X 2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) → A 2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2, +)) is used for magneto-optical trapping [3, 4] and Λ-cooling/imaging [5]. This is sent via six laser beams propagating along ±ˆx, ±ˆy, ±ˆz. Sidebands addressing the hyperﬁne manifolds are added using acousto-optical modulators (AOMs). These six laser beams also contain v = 1 vibrational repumping light (X 2Σ(v = 1, N = 1) →A 2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2, +)) with hyperﬁne sidebands added using EOMs. The cooling beam propagating along −ˆz passes through a 70:30 beamsplitter and exits the high-resolution microscope ob-

jective as a collimated beam. During magneto-optical trapping, Λ-cooling and imaging, v = 2, 3 vibrational repumping light (X 2Σ+(v = 2, 3, N = 1) →A 2Π1/2(v = 1, 2, J = 1/2, +)) enter along the molecular beam axis ˆx′, which is oriented 45 degrees with respect to ˆx and ˆy (Fig. S1).

## II. PREPARING SINGLE MOLECULES IN OPTICAL TWEEZER TRAPS

## A. Magneto-Optical Trapping and Sub-Doppler cooling

We start with a molecular beam of CaF molecules generated in a cryogenic buﬀer gas source (CBGB) [6] and it is slowed on the X −B transition via chirp slowing [7]. Slowed molecules are then loaded into a DC magneto-optical trap (MOT) [4], which is subsequently compressed [8, 9]. The molecules are then released and laser-cooled to sub-Doppler temperatures via Λ-cooling [5, 9, 10]. Details can be found in the supplemental material of [1].

## B. ODT Loading and Transport

After the molecules are magneto-optically trapped, we switch oﬀthe MOT and simultaneously turn on an attractive optical dipole trap (ODT) formed with 1064 nm

To increase the total trap depth, the beam is retro-reﬂected to form a 1D lattice using a cat-eye setup. Following release from the MOT, we apply 2 ms of Λ-cooling at high intensities and small blue detunings. Subsequently, the Λ-cooling parameters are then adjusted to those optimal for loading molecules into the ODT. Over the next ∼100 ms, molecules are loaded into the ODT in the presence of Λ-cooling [5, 10–12]. Maximal transfer of molecules from the Λ-cooled cloud to the ODT is achieved when the ODT overlaps with the center of the Λ-cooled cloud. The location of the optical tweezer array, on the other hand, is deﬁned by the optical axis and focal plane of the microscope objective, which is displaced from the MOT center by ≈500 µm along ˆx′ and ˆz (Fig. S1). Since this distance is much larger than the radial width of the ODT-trapped molecules (1/e2 width of ∼20 µm), a transport step is needed. To transport the molecules, we directly move the position of the ODT after it has been loaded with molecules. In detail, the ODT beam is sent through a 2-axis acoustooptical deﬂector (AOD) before entering the chamber. By ramping the frequencies of the rf tones driving each axis of the AOD, we move the ODT from its initial location, centered on the MOT, to its ﬁnal location in the focal plane of the optical tweezer array. The rf frequencies are chirped linearly over 30 ms.

## C. Loading Molecules into Optical Tweezer Traps

To load molecules into the optical tweezer traps, the optical tweezers are turned on following ODT transport at a depth of V = kB × 0.68(12) mK. Λ-cooling light is then applied using the MOT beams along ˆx, ˆy, ˆz for 75 ms. Subsequently, the ODT power is ramped down over 5 ms and molecules that are not loaded into tweezers fall away over the next 15 ms. The optimal parameters for the Λ-cooling light during tweezer loading is separately optimized. The single-photon detuning is ∆= 39 MHz, and the two-photon detuning is δ = 0 MHz. The hyper- ﬁne power ratio between the F = 2 and F = 1−hyperﬁne components is R2,1 = 2.1.

## III. GENERATING AN ARRAY OF OPTICAL TWEEZER TRAPS

The optical tweezer traps are generated from light near 780 nm, focused to near-diﬀraction-limited spots through a microscope objective with maximum numerical aperture of 0.65. For all data presented, we use a 1D array of 20 optical tweezers, formed from 20 regularly-spaced diﬀracted spots from an AOD. The frequency spacing for the AOD is set at 1 MHz, which corresponds to an optical tweezer spacing of 4.1 µm.

The powers of the optical tweezer beams are balanced for uniformity. We measure the intensities of the tweezer beams at an intermediate image plane before they enter the objective, and adjust the intensities by changing the power of the RF tones fed to the AOD. The measured intensities at the intermediate plane are balanced to better than 1%. The balancing is separately veriﬁed by diﬀerential ac Stark shift measurements on the X −B transition, which show a standard deviation of ≈10% over all 20 tweezers. This is limited by the precision of the diﬀerential ac Stark shift measurements.

## A. Imaging Setup

In the main text, two methods of imaging are described: 1) single-color Λ-imaging with Λ-cooling light on the X −A transition, and 2) bichromatic imaging

consisting of Λ-cooling light along with light addressing the X 2Σ+(v = 0, N = 1, F = 0) −B 2Σ+(v = 0, N = 0) transition. For Λ-imaging, we use the six beams along ±ˆx, ±ˆy and ±ˆz. Each beam has two hyperﬁne components nominally addressing the X(v = 0, N = 1, F = 1−, 2) hyper- ﬁne manifolds. For bichromatic imaging, we additionally add four small beams (≈2 mm diameter) propagating mostly along ±ˆx, ±ˆy addressing the X 2Σ+(v = 0, N = 1, F = 0)−B 2Σ+(v = 0, N = 0) transition. Due to optical access constraints, these beams have a small vertical component. The plane spanned by these beams intersect the x-y plane at ∼5◦. For imaging, X −B ﬂuorescence at 531 nm is collected through the microscope objective and imaged onto an EMCCD camera. The microscope objective is apochromatic and has a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.65. Due to apertures behind the objective, the working NA is slightly reduced. This reduction is not axially symmetric. Using the exact geometry of the apertures, we numerically compute the reduction factor to the overall collection eﬃciency. To ﬁlter out the large amount of Λ-cooling light (606 nm) and v = 1 light (628 nm) that propagates and scatters along ±ˆz, two dichroic ﬁlters that pass 531 nm light but ﬁlter out 606 nm and 628 nm light are placed in the imaging path. Taking into account the transmission of the objective, the eﬀective aperture size, the transmissions of the vacuum window, various compensation optics, beamsplitters and dichroic beamsplitters, the overall eﬃciency of the photon detection is 0.049(2). This also takes into account the quantum eﬃciency of the camera and the reﬂection of the camera window.

## B. Double-Imaging Procedure

For each experimental run, we image the molecules twice sequentially using bichromatic imaging (Fig. S3(a)). ## VI. FIDELITY ESTIMATION

In this section, we describe in detail how we extract classiﬁcation errors, the imaging ﬁdelity and the nondestructive detection ﬁdelity.

## A. Classiﬁcation Errors

Classiﬁcation errors are of two types: occupied tweezer sites identiﬁed as empty, and empty sites identiﬁed as occupied. We denote these errors as follows: ϵ10 is the probability of classifying an occupied tweezer site (at the beginning of the imaging pulse) to be empty; ϵ01 is the probability of classifying an empty tweezer site (at the beginning of the imaging pulse) to be occupied. We note that these errors depend on the threshold θ used for classiﬁcation. From the two errors, ϵ10 and ϵ01, one ﬁnds that the total error ϵ is given by ϵ = pϵ10 + (1 −p)ϵ01. This is dependent both on the the threshold θ and the true tweezer occupation probability p.

## B. Deﬁnition of Imaging Fidelity

We ﬁrst deﬁne the occupation-dependent detection ﬁ- delity fdet(p) = Maxθ(1 −ϵ) as the maximum ﬁdelity (minimum total error) achieved for a given a tweezer occupation probability p, optimized over all thresholds θ. We note that both the detection ﬁdelity fdet(p) and the optimal threshold is also a function of p. For example, for p = 1, fdet(1) = 1 can be achieved with θ = 0. To provide an occupation-independent metric for detection ﬁdelity, we deﬁne the imaging ﬁdelity f as the detection ﬁdelity obtained for p = 0.5, i.e. f = fdet(p = 0.5). We note that fdet(0.5) is typically lower than fdet(p ≈1) or fdet(p ≈0).

## D. Error Model and Imaging Fidelity Extraction

To estimate the imaging ﬁdelity, we ﬁrst determine the errors ϵ10(θ) and ϵ01(θ) as a function of the threshold θ. The errors ϵ10(θ) and ϵ01(θ) can be determined if we know the histogram for an empty tweezer and the histogram for an occupied tweezer. While one can create empty tweezers by not loading molecules, creating occupied tweezers with 100% probability directly is not possible, since the tweezer loading process is stochastic. To obtain the histogram for an occupied tweezer, we make use of the double-imaging procedure described in Section V B, followed by a subtraction procedure during image analysis. For each experimental run, we load molecules into the 20 tweezers stochastically, and then take two consecutive images (Fig. S3(a)). The two images have imaging durations of 10 ms and 30 ms, respectively, with the ﬁrst image intended to be minimally destructive. We next create a series of post-selected histograms from the second image conditioned upon camera counts exceeding a series of classiﬁcation threshold θ1 in the ﬁrst image (Fig. S3). When creating histograms, we treat all 20 tweezers to be identical. Diﬀerent values of θ1 lead to diﬀerent post-selected histograms corresponding to different tweezer loading rates.

As shown in Fig. S4(a), the post-selected histograms are bimodal. At suﬃciently large thresholds θ1, the post-selected normalized histograms display a suppressed lower peak. However, a small peak corresponding to a small fraction of unoccupied sites is still visible. In order to obtain the histogram from an occupied tweezer, we subtract oﬀthis small contribution with the following procedure. Over a range of θ1 where the lower peak is suppressed but suﬃcient data remains to provide acceptable signalto-noise ratios, we create normalized cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) g(θ2) from the histograms. As shown in Fig. S4(b), one observes that the CDF rises abruptly at a threshold θthres, and then increases approximately linearly above the threshold. This linear portion corresponds to a ﬂat histogram distribution near zero photon counts, which arises because of the ﬁnite imaging lifetime [15]. The sharp rise near θthres in the CDF corresponds to the small unoccupied peak. We remove this contribution by ﬁtting the linear portion of the CDF, and replacing the non-linear portion near θthres with a ﬁtted linear curve truncated at θthres (Fig. S4(d)). As shown in Fig. S4(e), this distribution, g′(θ2), contains a jump at θthres, which corresponds to the area under the lower peak in the imaging histogram. In the ﬁnal step, we subtract this jump and normalize the CDF to obtain the true CDF g′′(θ2) for occupied tweezers. Speciﬁcally, we subtract g′(θthres) from g′(θ2) and rescale the resulting curve such that g′′(∞) = 1 (Fig. S4(e)). We note that g′′(θ2) in fact coincides with ϵ10(θ2), the probability of classifying an occupied site as empty for a classiﬁcation threshold θ2. The normalized histogram for an occupied tweezer, h(θ2) can be obtained by taking the derivative of g′′(θ2) with respect to θ2 (Fig. S4(h)). To obtain ϵ01, we use the histogram for an unoccupied tweezer. This can be accomplished simply by shifting the region about each tweezer to be be suﬃciently far away from the tweezer position (10 binned camera pixels (2x2 binning), 7.2 µm away). The resulting histograms simulate unoccupied tweezers with similar background light as the imaging regions for the tweezers. The function ϵ01(θ2) can then be obtained by summing the number of counts above θ2, and normalizing by the total number of counts.

## VII. THERMOMETRY

To measure the temperature of the molecules in the tweezer trap, we perform release and recapture measurements. In detail, following the ﬁrst image, where the initial occupations of each tweezer trap are determined, the tweezer traps are switched oﬀabruptly and the molecules are released. After a variable hold time, during which the molecular samples expand, the tweezer traps are then abruptly switched on. The fraction of molecules recaptured is subsequently measured. The release-andrecapture curves are normalized to the survival fraction at zero release time. The release-and-recapture curves are then ﬁt to classical Monte Carlo simulations with diﬀerent initial molecular temperatures. The simulations assume an ideal Gaussian trap with beam waist w0 = 720(14) nm and trap depth V = kB × 1.28(11) mK. Gravity is also included in the simulation. In detail, molecules are ﬁrst initialized from a thermal distribution ignoring the small eﬀect of gravity. The temperature of this sample is obtained by directly computing the kinetic energy, and using the Virial theorem for a harmonic trap kBT = 1 2m v2 , which is expected to be valid when kBT ≪V . The abrupt release and recapture sequence is then simulated. Following recapture, we evolve the system for 5 ms to ensure that untrapped molecules fall away. We then obtain the ﬁnal fraction of molecules that remain in the trap by counting molecules remaining in the region deﬁned by r < 3w0, |z| < 3zR. This produces simulated releaseand-recapture curves. The experimental data is then ﬁt to the simulated data with two free parameters, the overall scale and the temperature. The uncertainties in the trap depth and beam waist are taken into account in the following way. Separate simulated data sets are produced with either w0 or V oﬀset by 1σ from its center value. The data is then ﬁt to these two curves. The deviations in the ﬁtted temperature are then added in quadrature to produce error bars.

## A. Measurement Procedure

As described in the main text, we measure the variation of the diﬀerential ac Stark shift between the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) and B2Σ(v = 0, N = 0) states as a function of the wavelength of the optical tweezer light. On the X −B light at 531 nm, four sidebands each addressing the four hyperﬁne levels in X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) are created using a phase modulator [2]. The tweezer depth is held constant, while a 5 ms pulse of 531 nm light illuminates the molecules. When the light is resonant with the Stark-shifted resonance, molecules are heated out of the tweezer. We detect the number of surviving molecules 30 ms following the illumination pulse. As a function of the overall detuning of the X −B spectroscopy light, we observe a single loss feature. The peak loss frequency as a function of the tweezer wavelength (λ) directly measures the average diﬀerential Stark shift between the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) and B2Σ(v = 0, N = 0) states. We assume that the measured shift is 1/2 of the peak diﬀerential ac Stark shift. To verify the linear dependence of the Stark shift with power, we measure the diﬀerential Stark shift versus tweezer power at λ = 781.1 nm and the magic wavelength of 782 nm. We ﬁnd that both curves scale linearly with power (Fig. S6(a)). Extrapolation to zero power allows us to calibrate the frequency of X −B light that corresponds to zero diﬀerential ac Stark shift.

## XII. RATE EQUATION MODEL FOR MODELING POPULATION DYNAMICS DURING IMAGING

We extract the parity-changing loss rate during bichromatic imaging through ﬁtting population dynamics measurements to a rate equation model. In this section, we describe in detail the rate equation model, and how the parameters of the model are determined. To enhance the eﬀect of parity-changing loss when the molecules are illuminated by X-B light, we make all population dynamic measurements at a higher X −B intensity of 24(2) mW/cm2, which is double the optimal bichromatic imaging X −B intensity. For detection, the X −B intensity is kept at the optimal value of 12(1) mW/cm2.

## A. Relevant States and Processes

In our rate equation model, the relevant states described are |X, v = 0, N = 0, J = 1/2, F = 1, mF = −1, 0, 1⟩, |X, v = 0, N = 0, J = 1/2, F = 0, mF = 0⟩, |X, v = 0, N = 1⟩, and |X, v = 0, N = 2⟩. These are denoted by N0,|1,mF ⟩, N0,|0,0⟩,N1, and N2, respectively. Note that we keep track of the populations in the |X, v = 0, N = 0, J = 1/2⟩hyperﬁne mF states separately, since some of our measurements either prepare or detect molecules in only one of these states. During bichromatic imaging, due to photon scattering, population can be transferred between or lost from the

above states. Our model captures the following population transfer and loss processes. First, bichromatic imaging empirically results in loss of molecules from the detectable X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) manifold. We denote the total imaging loss rate by Γimg, which we directly measure. This loss rate includes all possible loss channels out of X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1), known and unknown. Second, we separately include parity-changing terms that arise from molecules decaying via the B →A → X pathway. During bichromatic imaging, molecules are excited on the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1, J = 1/2, F = 0) − B2Σ(v = 0, N = 0, J = 1/2) transition. The excited molecules can subsequently decay either directly to X2Σ or via the two-photon pathways B2Σ →A2ΠΩ→X, where Ω= 1/2, 3/2. In the latter processes, the parity of the molecules is changed upon returning to X2Σ, and the molecules end up in X2Σ(N = 0) or X2Σ(N = 2). We describe these in detail in Section XII A 1. Third, during imaging, oﬀ-resonant photon scattering also leads to population transfer between various evenparity ground rotational states X2Σ(v = 0, N = 0, 2). The dominant process is Λ-cooling light that is resonant with the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) →A2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2, +) transition, oﬀ-resonantly addressing the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 0, 2) → A2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2, 3/2, 5/2, 7/2, −). We take into account oﬀ-resonant transitions to states in the A2Π1/2(v = 0) manifold. We will describe these in detail in Section XII A 2 and Section XII A 3. There are three other much slower processes that occur, which are not included in the rate equation model. These three processes are as follows. First, Raman scattering of the tweezer light can lead to rotational mixing of the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 0) and X2Σ(v = 0, N = 2) states, and also further loss into higher rotational states with even N. We have measured that this occur on timescales much longer than the explored internal dynamics here. Second, loss to X2Σ(v = 1) can also occur due to blackbody radiation, but is expected to occur on a much longer timescale (observed to be ∼5 s). Third, losses due to collision with background gas leads to state-independent loss. Lifetime measurements of X2Σ(N = 1) molecules indicate that this occurs on a much longer timescale even when compared to blackbody excitation.

2. Oﬀ-Resonant Scattering Processes

The nominally dark X2Σ(v = 0, N = 0, 2) manifolds experience oﬀ-resonant scattering from the bichromatic imaging light. Predominantly, the bichromatic imaging light consists of Λ-cooling light addressing the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) →A2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2, +) transition and vibrational repumping light addressing the X2Σ(v = 1, N = 1) →A2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2, +) transition. ## C. Determining Rate Equation Parameters

1. Determining Overall Imaging Loss Rate

To make progress, we ﬁrst measure the overall imaging loss rate Γimg at the X −B intensity used for all population measurements. This intensity is twice that used for the detection images, in order to enhance the relative contribution of parity-changing loss. The imaging loss rate is obtained by measuring the remaining X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) population versus imaging time. By ﬁtting the data to an exponentially decaying curve, we obtain Γimg = 14.1(16) s−1 (Fig. S11(a)).

2. Determining Oﬀ-Resonant Scattering Rate

We next determine the various oﬀ-resonant scattering rates. Since the oﬀ-resonant scattering rates are all related by their respective detunings and Honl-London factors, we can express all oﬀ-resonant scattering rates to Γ0l. To determine Γ0l, we ﬁrst prepare molecules in |X, v = 0, N = 0, F = 1, mF = 1⟩. Next, we illuminate them with bichromatic imaging light for variable durations, before detecting the remaining population in |X, v = 0, N = 0, F = 1, mF = 1⟩. In detail, molecules loaded into the tweezers are ﬁrst imaged with bichromatic light for 10 ms to determine their initial occupation. Subsequently, an optical pumping pulse pumps a fraction of molecules into |X, v = 0, N = 1, J = 1/2, F = 0⟩. We then perform a Landau-Zener microwave frequency sweep at a magnetic ﬁeld of 4.3 G to transfer |X, v = 0, N = 1, J = 1/2, F = 0⟩ molecules into |X, v = 0, N = 0, J = 1/2, F = 1, mF = 1⟩. Subsequently, a short (2 ms) pulse of light resonant with X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) →A2Π(v = 0, J = 1/2, +) removes all remaining population in the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) manifold. To detect the remaining population in |X, v = 0, N = 0, F = 1, mF = 1⟩, a reverse microwave sweep on the |X, v = 0, N = 1, J = 1/2, F = 0⟩ → |X, v = 0, N = 0, J = 1/2, F = 1, mF = 1⟩is applied to bring molecules back into the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) manifold, which is subsequently detected with a 30 ms long imaging pulse. As shown in Fig. S11(b), under bichromatic imaging, the |X, v = 0, N = 0, J = 1/2, F = 1, mF = 1⟩ population decays rapidly over 20 ms. To provide further information on the population dynamics, we perform a second measurement, where population in all |X, v = 0, N = 0, F = 1, mf⟩ states are detected. In detail, after the variable bichromatic imaging pulse, three mi-

crowave sweeps are performed sequentially on the |X, v = 0, N = 0, J = 1/2, F = 1, mF = −1, 0, 1⟩ → |X, v = 0, N = 1, J = 1/2, F = 0⟩transitions, and interspersed with a short “depumping” pulse (50 µs) resonant with the |X, v = 0, N = 1, J = 1/2, F = 0⟩→ A2Π1/2, v = 0, J = 1/2, + transition. The depumping pulse optically pumps molecules out of the X(v = 0, N = 1, F = 0) state into the other X(v = 0, N = 1) states. As shown in Fig. S11(c), in this second measurement, we observe a rapid decay over ∼20 ms, followed by a long decay over ∼300 ms.

Having determined Γimg and all the oﬀ-resonant scattering rates, we next determine the parity-changing rate Γparity. We prepare molecules in the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) manifold and perform bichromatic imaging for a variable amount of time. Next, X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) molecules are removed using a short resonant pulse of imaging light (2 ms). We next transfer molecules from the |X(v = 0), N = 0, F = 1, mF ⟩states into the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) manifold via microwave sweeps interspersed with depumping pulses (described in previous section). The ﬁnal X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) population is measured. As shown in Fig. S11(d), the detected population is initially zero. In order to ﬁt to the rate equation model, we need to determine the overall scale, i.e. what fraction of initially identiﬁed molecules are in fact available to use in the measurement, and what fraction of remaining molecules are detected. We separately measure overall survival eﬃciencies and state transfer eﬃciencies. Based on the initial detected fraction in the N = 1 lifetime measurement, we estimate that 0.55(3) of the tweezers initially identiﬁed as occupied in the ﬁrst image are subsequently detected. This takes into account loss during the ﬁrst image, classiﬁcation errors in the ﬁrst and second images, and any other loss between the two images that occurs due to technical heating and collisions with background gas. The lower fraction than the optimal non-destructive detection ﬁ- delity is in part due to classiﬁcation errors in the second image, and also an intentionally higher classiﬁcation threshold used in the second image. The higher threshold is used to minimize false positives, which could lead to an oﬀset. Second, we measure the eﬃciency of the microwave sweep used to bring molecules into N = 1 for detection.
